title: Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 scores S-plus on coding but is "not at the frontier" for writing, reviewer says
text:
Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 scores S-plus on coding but is "not at the frontier" for writing, reviewer says — BigGo Finance Ask AI Real-time News Market Earnings Call Event Calendar Watchlist Podcast Market Influencers Earnings Call Event Calendar Watchlist Podcast Market Influencers More Ask AI Real-time News Watchlist Holdings Market Earnings Call Event Calendar Podcast Market Influencers Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 scores S-plus on coding but is "not at the frontier" for writing, reviewer says
 Add preferred source Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 is a "paradigm shift" model for ambitious, hand-off work — one tester used it to build a full video editor that would normally cost millions — but it is slow, expensive, and mediocre for everyday writing, according to Every's Dan Shipper, who tested the model on launch day. The strongest evidence is EveryCut, a video editor replicating Premiere, Descript and StreamYard, built end-to-end by prompting in a couple of weeks for thousands of dollars in tokens. A research documentary cost about 1.4 billion tokens, roughly $2,000 at Fable 5.1 rates or $862 at Opus 5.5 rates. Shipper's verdict is deliberately narrow: S-plus for coding, S for a knowledge worker who restructures how they work, B for anyone using it on email and documents, and B to B-plus for prose that "buries the lead" and trails Gemini 4 Argon. The market implication is economic rather than technical. Fable 5.2's best use cases are priced for companies and heavy token users today, which keeps cheaper models like Opus 5.5 as the everyday workhorse — and gives incumbent software vendors such as Adobe a window to re-justify their value before custom-built tools get cheap. Shipper expects that window to close within six months to a year. Key Elements 
 Anthropic Claude Fable 5.2 Claude Opus 5.5 Claude Mythos 5.2 Dan Shipper Every EveryCut Kieran Klaassen Mike Taylor Tyler Nishida Adobe Premiere Gemini 4 Argon Claude Code Anthropic's newest model is not the best at most things. That is precisely why it matters.
 Dan Shipper, who leads AI product coverage at Every, spent launch day testing Claude Fable 5.2 across coding, research, design and writing, and landed on a verdict that is more useful than a benchmark score: the model is "spiky." On a narrow set of ambitious, long-running tasks it is the best tool he has used. On everything routine, it is the wrong choice — too slow, too expensive, too greedy with tokens. "The best measure of a new model is whether it causes you to try things that you never would have tried before," he said, speaking on the Every podcast. "And by that measure, Claude Fable 5.2 is a true paradigm shift of a model."
 That framing is the whole argument. Fable 5.2 does not win by being uniformly better. It wins by making a category of work possible that previously required a team, a budget, and several months.
 A video editor, built by prompting
 The flagship evidence came from Every frontier team member Kieran Klaassen, who receives early model access and tests it on the company's actual work. Klaassen built EveryCut, a fully featured video editor, end-to-end by prompting. It includes an agent, transcription of everything on screen, recording, and editing — combining features Every previously pulled from Premiere, Descript and StreamYard into a single internal tool.
 Shipper's point is not that this is a fun demo. It is that the economics of professional software just moved. "Now anyone can make their own professional software for their work if they want to," he said. "And I think that changes the game both for companies and for software vendors."
 He is careful to distinguish this from cheap "vibe coding." EveryCut cost roughly thousands of dollars in tokens. But Shipper says it would normally have required millions of dollars of investment — and it took a couple of weeks instead of a product cycle. Klaassen also built his own Ableton-style music tool, and found Fable 5.2 used the model's "ultracode" mode better than any prior release: trustworthy rather than risky, where earlier models would burn tokens on unwanted extras.
 The workflow this implies is asynchronous. Designer Tyler Nishida calls it an "overnight model" or a "need a new computer model." Shipper pushed work to a cloud Mac Mini and came back hours later to finished results. Fable 5.2 is the first model he has seen that gives an ETA — "I think this will be done at 6:30 p.m." — and in one case it warned Nishida to plug in his laptop because the battery would die before the task finished.
 The gaming results are the most vivid illustration. Staff editor Jack Cheng's standing benchmark uploads a photo of toys on his kids' bedroom floor and asks the model to build a game from them. Against a rival model called Astra, the Astra version was "reasonable," but the car could only go left and right with no throttle control. Fable 5.2 produced a Mario Kart-style racer with selectable characters drawn from the actual toys — Sunny, Blaze, Scoop — off-track driving, a spring item, and "press X to use your item" mechanics. Shipper's advice to anyone who wants to make games: "run, not walk" to this model.
 The knowledge-work gain is structural, not cosmetic
 Shipper splits knowledge work sharply in two. For ordinary tasks — documents, email, routine admin — the model is, in his words, "way too powerful": slow, expensive, and token-hungry. He says plainly not to use it there. For people rethinking what knowledge work actually is, he rates it S tier and says it "will absolutely change your life."
 The example is Mike Taylor, Every's head of evals. Tasked with a research project on getting AI to write like him, Taylor would normally have produced a Notion doc or a slide deck. Instead he recorded himself talking about the work, and Fable 5.2 cut it into a documentary explaining what he did, why it matters, and what he found. Shipper's framing: the model takes communication "from being black and white to being like HD full color." He expects most companies to be communicating internally through videos, custom apps and podcasts within a couple of years.
 Taylor's second gain was structural. His research resembles model training: rather than setting up each experiment himself, he handed experiment ideas to the model, ran them in parallel overnight, and had results by end of day while doing other parts of his job. Taylor called it the most productive three weeks of his career, compressing months of research into a couple of weeks. Shipper calls him "a canary in the coal mine" for the future knowledge-worker workflow.
 The constraint is price. Exact Fable 5.2 pricing was unknown as of recording, so Shipper used Fable 5.1 rates as a proxy. One explainer documentary consumed roughly 1.4 billion tokens — about $2,000 at Fable 5.1 rates, or $862 at Opus 5.5 rates. His read: at these prices, such workflows are out of reach unless you are a large company or "token rich." But he expects them to become very cheap within six months to a year.
 Where it fails: prose with a superiority complex
 Writing is the weak spot. Shipper gives it a B to B-plus. Staff writer Katie, who runs Every's "Vibe Checks," found Fable 5.2 has the easiest-to-read prose of any model she has tested, with genuine emotional awareness and humor. She also called it "a smug know it all," condescending in the manner of Sonnet 5.5, and prone to stopping too early at medium effort levels.
 Shipper agrees, and ranks rivals well above it: Gemini 4 Argon is "by far better" at writing, with Astra a close second. His specific complaint about the Anthropic line is journalistic — it does not put the interesting thing at the top. It buries the lead, and it makes connections to things that are not real. His summary: for all the model's intelligence, plain text communication "is just not at the frontier."
 Design: a new ceiling, if you tune the effort dial
 Design earns an A. Nishida called Fable 5.2 "a new ceiling for models" — easy to talk to, and a level above Opus. The caveat is calibration: at higher effort levels it does "a little bit too much," while lower effort levels are pleasant.
 Shipper's illustration is his standing test of making a movie of Plato's Protagoras . Fable 5.2 gave Socrates a black beard — correct, because Socrates is in his thirties in that dialogue — where every other model defaults to the gray-haired, balding representation. Shipper treats this as evidence of the detail fidelity Claude models get right, and his general guidance for this class of model is to tune effort levels rather than switch between model tiers.
 The scorecard, and the colleague analogy
 Shipper's overall rating is S tier, but the organizing idea is spikiness — extraordinary on a narrow set of ambitious tasks, ordinary elsewhere. On some coding tasks it beat Astra 6, but Astra 6 was far faster and more token-efficient.
 Category Tier Note 
 Overall S Paradigm-shifting but spiky 
 Coding S-plus Changes what is possible in software engineering 
 Knowledge work S for the right person, B otherwise Slow, expensive, token-hungry for routine use 
 Design A New ceiling, watch effort levels 
 Writing B / B-plus Readable but buries the lead; behind Gemini 4 Argon and Astra 
 Klaassen's division of labor is the practical takeaway: Opus 5.5 when you are in the loop, Fable 5.2 for hand-off. Mike, Every's head of evals, put it more memorably. Fable is "a rare senior colleague that you want to use deliberately," while Opus feels "a little bit more like a $30 an hour Upwork contractor" you can use for everything.
 What Anthropic is claiming, and what it is not proving
 Anthropic's own launch materials push the same theme harder. The company says Fable 5.2 and its restricted sibling Mythos 5.2 — the latter limited at launch to vetted organizations — completed software migrations previously considered infeasible, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, resolved two open problems in black hole physics, and formalized a proof of Fermat's Last Theorem in 30 hours. The 5.2 releases arrive roughly two months after the September launch of Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1.
 Notably, Anthropic did not provide detailed benchmarks or independent verification of those results. That gap is exactly why Every's day-zero testing exists. The frontier team gets models from all major labs before release and tests them on real work — coding, writing, design, general knowledge work — rather than public benchmarks or demo clips. Every receives free tokens as part of that access, which Shipper discloses, while stating the opinions are the company's own.
 The context around the launch is also instructive. Anthropic recently had to loosen restrictions in Claude Code after a rule meant to stop game cloning swept up original titles that merely borrowed familiar mechanics. Engineer Addy Osmani acknowledged the rule went too far; the fix, shipped in version 2.1.317, lets developers name a reference game and describe the mechanics they want, with the model expected to build something original instead. The episode followed a public demonstration of how fast this generation of models moves: Mark Brown of Game Maker's Toolkit watched a Claude Code-made clone of his own Word Play game appear in about 12 minutes, against the seven months he spent building the original.
 That is the backdrop against which Fable 5.2's game-development strength lands. The capability is real. The policy scaffolding around it is still being written.
 For investors, the signal is not another model leaderboard shuffle. It is a pricing question with a clock attached. Fable 5.2's best use cases — a $2,000 documentary, a thousands-of-dollars internal video editor, overnight agentic coding runs — are today affordable only to companies and heavy token users. Shipper's forecast that these workflows become very cheap within six months to a year is the claim worth tracking. If it holds, the "spiky" model becomes the default, and the case for keeping a cheaper workhorse like Opus 5.5 as the everyday driver weakens. It also means the pressure on incumbent software vendors such as Adobe — whose Premiere feature set Klaassen effectively rebuilt by asking — is not a one-off stunt but a preview. Until then, the operating rule is simple: route ambitious, hand-off work to Fable 5.2, and keep faster, cheaper models for anything interactive or routine.
